section_summary: This section documents U.S. efforts to suppress Japanese propaganda publications in wartime Argentina and to distribute post-surrender Japanese newspapers among Japanese communities in Brazil and Peru. It also contains reports on the democratization, ownership, management, labor disputes, editorial policy, finances, circulation, and equipment of the Yomiuri newspaper under the Allied Occupation. A separate airgram reports British parliamentary concern about the speed and adequacy of press information reaching the United Kingdom Liaison Mission in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Telegram 2073 on closure of Japanese publications in Argentina
subfiles.from: Spruille Braden, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports an Argentine decree closing identified Japanese publications and printing establishments.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 2073: Argentina decreed September 4 the closure of listed Japanese publications and print shops; Die Zeitung's non-closure is being raised with the Foreign Office.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese newspapers to the American Mission at Lima
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge of the American Mission, Lima
subfiles.about: Transmits post-surrender Tokyo newspapers for discretionary distribution among Japanese residents of Peru.
subfiles.summary: Department sends Japanese newspapers to Lima, as São Paulo requested them to show Brazil's Japanese community Japan's defeat, since Peru's Japanese may not know of the surrender.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Japanese newspapers to the Consulate General at São Paulo
subfiles.to: American Consular Officer in Charge, São Paulo
subfiles.about: Forwards current Tokyo newspapers for distribution within Brazil's Japanese community and requests an evaluation of their effect.
subfiles.summary: Department sends São Paulo newspapers from the Political Adviser, asks for an assessment of their influence, and notes relief shipments to Japan remain unresolved.

subfiles.title: Despatch 106: Transmission of Japanese Newspapers for Distribution to Japanese Colonies in South America
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., Acting United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards post-surrender Tokyo newspapers and recommends distributing them among Japanese communities in Brazil and Peru.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson responds to reports that Japanese community leaders in Brazil wanted current newspapers from Japan. He suggests giving part of the collection to the embassy in Lima as well, arguing that the papers would demonstrate Japan's defeat and democratization and would therefore have a beneficial propaganda effect in Latin America.

subfiles.title: Despatch 341: Reappearance of Japanese Press in Argentina
subfiles.from: Spruille Braden, U.S. Embassy, Buenos Aires
subfiles.about: Reports the reappearance in Spanish of Japanese newspapers suspended after Argentina declared war on Japan.
subfiles.summary: Braden reports that two of three suspended Japanese-language dailies had resumed publication in Spanish and that one had tested clandestine Japanese publication in June. He urges renewed closure under inter-American anti-Axis resolutions, warning that the newspapers could preserve community cohesion, disseminate propaganda, and facilitate espionage.

subfiles.title: Note Verbale concerning suppression of Japanese propaganda in Argentina
subfiles.to: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Worship of the Argentine Republic
subfiles.about: Requests action against Japanese newspapers, magazines, printing shops, a church bulletin, and alleged propagandists in Argentina.
subfiles.summary: Note verbale: the embassy names Sol de Mañana and Senda as successors to Japanese-language papers and urges liquidating their activities, seizing records and type, with names, addresses and propagandists, citing the Act of Chapultepec and Rio resolution.

subfiles.title: Despatch 172: Report on the Yomiuri-Hochi
subfiles.from: George Atcheson Jr., United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a SCAP report and news article concerning the employee-led transformation of Yomiuri-Hochi.
subfiles.summary: Atcheson describes Yomiuri-Hochi's rapid change from an ultramilitarist, pro-Axis newspaper under Matsutaro Shoriki into a leading liberal daily controlled by its employees. He notes Shoriki's arrest designation, Tsunego Baba's accession to the presidency, Tomin Suzuki's influence, growing circulation, and the paper's attacks on mythologized Japanese history.

subfiles.title: Special Report on Yomiuri-Hochi Newspaper
subfiles.from: Civil Censorship Detachment, Office of the Chief of Counter Intelligence, U.S. Army Forces Pacific
subfiles.about: Analyzes Yomiuri-Hochi's history, ownership, finances, organization, wartime policy, and employee seizure of control.
subfiles.summary: The report traces the origins and merger of Hochi and Yomiuri and describes Shoriki's success in building circulation through sensational reporting and promotional innovations. It details ownership, finances, organization, censorship of liberal material, and the October 1945 employee revolt encouraged by SCAP press-freedom directives. It also lists executives stripped of practical authority, technical personnel and neutrals still working, and union-aligned employees exercising actual control.

subfiles.title: Employees Gain Victory in Yomiuri Dispute
subfiles.about: Reports the settlement of the seven-week Yomiuri labor and management dispute in favor of the employees.
subfiles.summary: Shoriki accepted most employee demands before entering Sugamo Prison: executives resign, Tsunego Baba appointed, employee management participation, union recognition and collective bargaining; seen as democratizing labor and journalism.

subfiles.title: Airgram A-520 on newspaper service to the United Kingdom Liaison Mission in Tokyo
subfiles.from: Lewis W. Douglas, U.S. Embassy, London
subfiles.about: Transmits British House of Commons questions and answers about newspaper delivery and press monitoring for the United Kingdom mission in Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Airgram A-520: William Teeling asks whether the British mission gets newspapers and press comment quickly; Bevin describes services provided; Teeling contrasts rapid monitoring the American ambassador reportedly gives MacArthur.

subfiles.title: Despatch 288: Transmittal of Special Report “The Yomiuri Newspaper”
subfiles.from: Acting United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards two copies of a SCAP research report on the recent history and organization of Yomiuri.
subfiles.summary: Despatch 288 sends the report 'The Yomiuri Newspaper': Japan's third-largest paper, Shoriki's presidency, Baba's succession, his conflict with chief editor Tomin Suzuki, and the employees' union.

subfiles.title: The Yomiuri Newspaper, Special Report AR-276-IM-95-PP-B-26
subfiles.from: Information Media Branch, Research Unit, Analysis and Research Division, Civil Information and Education Section, SCAP
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed institutional history and analysis of the Yomiuri Newspaper Publishing Company and its employees' union.
subfiles.summary: The report reconstructs Yomiuri's development under Shoriki, the employees' 1945 seizure of control, Baba's appointment, and the later conflict that ended with Suzuki's dismissal and creation of an independent union. It analyzes the company's legal structure, ownership, organization, finances, personnel, editorial policy, news sources, distribution, and equipment. Financial statements and circulation data document its postwar operations, while Appendix B begins reproducing the October 1946 labor contract; the contract continues beyond this section.
